title: SurePoint's New CEO Jeff Steinberg on the Mandate for Change
author: Jeff Steinberg

st.an: Steinberg identifies AI-infused workflows as an inflection point for rethinking law-firm operations and legal practice, but provides no evidence or argument about in-house adoption, selective insourcing, stronger corporate buyers, or changes in outside-counsel demand.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Steinberg accepts the need for cautious, context-sensitive deployment and extends the cluster’s operating-model thesis with a concrete product approach: combine technology with services, map functionality to distinct users, and preserve workflow flexibility across firms and governance models. He does not substantively address verification or general legal competence.
qs: At the same time, the mandate is in in my belief Is that technology alone is not sufficient.
We've got to have commonality, but we do have to understand that different firms and different partners need flexibility in their workflows to be able  to ~ be able to focus in.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Steinberg supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI creates an opportunity to rethink legal workflows and firm operations, with integrated information flows and efficiency as central goals. His position is broad and predictive, however, and does not materially address pricing pressure, apprenticeship, verification or buyer-side incentives.
qs: that that we put on to to things and that infuses the workflows creates an inflection point for people to rethink how their businesses operate, how they practice law, and how it goes forward.

So, you know, as we think about firm performance, we think about how you marry what's going on in in front of the the attorney, the partner, and the customer of the firm, and then how that flows seamlessly to the the administrative team.

st.t: Legal consolidation: Acquisitions create integration work first
st.an: Steinberg supports the cluster’s proposition that legal-tech strategy requires assembling capabilities through partnerships, acquisitions and organic development, with integration work preceding coherent customer value. He distinguishes technology, service and data partnerships, acknowledges SurePoint’s unfinished integration, and conditions acquisitions on customer value rather than treating transactions as successful outcomes.
qs: The the ecosystem in the legal industry is too broad for any one company to do everything all themselves.
So so we need to do more work integrating.

st.t: Legal leadership: Business capability complements legal expertise
st.an: Steinberg supports the proposition through a personal account of seeking operating experience to improve his business understanding and identifying law firms’ need for actionable metrics. His evidence reinforces the value of business and operational capability alongside professional expertise, though it does not address people management, outside expertise or measured performance outcomes.

st.an: Steinberg supports the cluster’s practical, implementation-led view: firms have uneven readiness, while adoption should remain tied to stable business needs and tools that are genuinely usable. His caution about shifting technology reinforces the synthesis’s rejection of capability-led transformation claims, though he does not directly address lawyer supervision or verification.

kp.k: AI creates an opportunity to rethink legal operations
kp.d: Steinberg presents AI-infused workflows and changing access to legal information as an inflection point for both legal practice and firm management. He predicts continuing technological change rather than the disappearance of legal practice, arguing that adjudication and negotiation will remain necessary. These are strategic expectations, not measured findings.
qs: All of the access to the law, the information, you know, all what this AI rubric. that that we put on to to things and that infuses the workflows creates an inflection point for people to rethink how their businesses operate, how they practice law, and how it goes forward.
So the practice of law never goes away. How we practice law may change.

kp.k: Machine learning and generative AI serve different proposed functions
kp.d: Steinberg proposes using machine learning to derive insights from historical facts and generative AI to communicate and contextualise those insights, including through visualisations. He frames reliable underlying data and business logic as essential to avoiding hallucinations and bad citations. The interview supplies no testing or performance evidence establishing that this architecture delivers the complete accuracy he seeks.
qs: So when you're mining the history and you need something to be a hundred percent accurate that's coming off a set of facts, ultimately you want the machine learning creating that insight.
In order for the user to consume it, you want generative AI on top of those insights.
And I think it's that balance between reliable output along with that probabilistic generative output to let me consume it better.
They're about a more deterministic approach. And I think we can apply the tools to both of those ~ so that we don't get hallucinations.

kp.k: Actionable insights require services as well as software
kp.d: Steinberg describes his leadership mandate as converting SurePoint's historical data into decisions and outcomes, supported by a larger service team. Better time capture with less effort is a proposed application, not a quantified result. He draws on Redwood's earlier combination of analytics technology and advisory services as a precedent for this approach.
qs: At the same time, the mandate is in in my belief Is that technology alone is not sufficient.
What firms really want is they want an ability to make good decisions and drive good outcomes, both in the practice and the business of law.
So we can help bring tools to timekeeping that improve the capture while reducing the time and effort involved in that time capture.
our customers should expect to see us continue to invest in a bigger, more robust team of people around the table.

kp.k: Early customer conversations reveal uneven AI adoption
kp.d: Speaking roughly ten days into the role, Steinberg reports that some firms have embraced AI while worrying about rapidly changing tools; others prefer a cautious approach shaped by practice area and circumstances. He says usability and tangible business value matter across these positions. This is an early anecdotal account without a reported sample size or systematic adoption measure; his target of five to ten customer conversations weekly is a plan, not completed research.
qs: you know, what we're hearing is that some firms have deeply embraced AI, but also have concerns about the fact that what AI was and the tools twelve months ago are different.
The business problem doesn't change. The business value doesn't change.
They want to measure twice and cut once type approach.
they know these are tools that are important to have, but they need them to be usable. They need them to be tangible.

kp.d: Steinberg argues that law-firm technology must evolve without disrupting lawyers and administrative staff. He describes customers ranging from 20 to 350 attorneys, with differences in offices, practice areas and operating models. His product goal combines a stable 10 to 20 year runway with faster evolution of insights; he contrasts relatively stable conflict checking and accounting entries with changing intelligence about clients and attorneys.
qs: And at the same time, the stability and the usability. for the attorneys and for the administrative team in law firms can't change too fast.
we we work with firms with 20 attorneys. We work with firms with 350 attorneys.
A really stable 10 to 20 year runway for somebody's firm performance software because people, once you go through the pain of changing, you don't want to have to change again.
conflict checking is not going to change, debit and credit entry is not going to change.

He says private-equity backing makes additional acquisitions an ongoing consideration but argues that these must add customer value. He links integration to reconsidering product purpose, particularly shifting beyond CRM toward marketing automation that helps partners communicate and generate matters.

we are private equity backed. ~ so we will always be thinking about logical value added acquisitions for our law firms.

That it's about providing value from the partners and the attorneys out to their customer bases, both to create awareness and to help drive additional matters and additional management.

kp.k: Integrated platforms still need role-specific workflow flexibility
kp.d: Asked about a common data layer and user experience, Steinberg advocates common functionality tailored to different users rather than specifying a technical architecture. Timekeepers and collections staff need different information and capabilities, while partners and firms vary in their degree of centralisation. He supports this view with a historical customer anecdote about providing shared services to 75 attorneys, 25 of whom were building their own books.
qs: A a timekeeper is a different user than the AR ~ and collections staff.

I've got 75 attorneys in the firm. 25 of them are building their own books of business. I have to provide a standard shared service, but Customized to what each one of those partners is trying to do in their own client base.
We've got to have commonality, but we do have to understand that different firms and different partners need flexibility in their workflows

kp.k: Partnerships complement acquisitions and internal technology
kp.d: Steinberg argues that no single legal-technology company can supply the entire ecosystem. He distinguishes technology, service and data partnerships, with acquisition or commercial collaboration depending partly on ownership preferences and the depth of integration needed. Strong API-based relationships may suffice in some cases; commercial partnerships can also evolve into business combinations.
qs: The the ecosystem in the legal industry is too broad for any one company to do everything all themselves.

I think about the technology partnerships that that we need to have. I think about the service partnerships that are critical to being able to provide the right support and and value to to our customers. And then I think about data partnerships
How important is it to really deeply integrate as opposed to being able to have good, strong relationships and have like APIs that move data back and forth?

kp.k: Midmarket technology must counter competing scale and agility advantages
kp.d: Steinberg describes midsized firms as pressured by larger firms' ability to spread acquisition, marketing, training and recruiting costs and by smaller firms' focus and nimbleness. He positions SurePoint's intended contribution as efficient front-to-back-office operations and profitable-growth insights, with unit costs matching or beating large firms while avoiding unnecessary large-firm functionality. These are competitive diagnoses and product objectives, not demonstrated cost savings.
qs: larger full service firms can spread acquisition costs, marketing costs, training costs, recruiting costs
they're also under pressure below with with the ~ firms that can be really focused and nimble.
We've got to be able to help them operate really, really efficiently at at a price point that gives them just as good, if not better, unit costs than large firms
but you don't need all of the, you know, multi currency ~ type functionality perhaps that a really large law firm needs to have

kp.k: Midmarket resilience complicates predictions of hollowing out
kp.d: Steinberg says midsized firms have proved more resilient than he expected, attributing this to strategies responsive to client preferences and how lawyers want to practise. He treats consolidation and lateral movement as longstanding trends, recalling discussion in 2006 and 2007, and characterises future change as uneven evolution. The host mentions SurePoint research, but no underlying study data are provided to substantiate the resilience assessment.
qs: I kind of expected the middle, like a lot of industries, to get hollowed a little bit,
And I think what we've seen is that the legal industry and law firms are resilient
Those were the same trends that that I was being asked about ~ when I was on ~ you know, ~ a panel at ILTA, you know, back in 2006, 2007.
but I think about it as as ~ evolution. as opposed to a a real dichotomy and and that evolution occurs in different paces in different ways.

kp.k: First-year priorities centre customers, product balance and implementation
kp.d: Steinberg sets three priorities for his first year: understanding the needs and preferred pace of change of partners, COOs, CFOs and attorneys; balancing long-term product stability with agility; and strengthening external partnerships and internal services so firms can understand and use insights. These are commitments for subsequent assessment, not completed achievements. His emphasis is on adoption and human support rather than technology alone.
qs: a lot of times technology companies fail because they get out in front of their customer and finding that right balance.
So number one, the the customers and clients and their needs. Number two, how the product balances those needs going forward.
And then the third is how do we bring a vibrant ecosystem of service partners and technology partners to our clients in the right way and build out our own services
So if the technology is great, if the insights are great, but we can't help them get to that knowledge in a in a seamless fashion ~ and understand it and use it, then we're not doing our jobs.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Steinberg predicts that AI will change law-firm operations and legal practice through efficiency improvements and evolving workflows, without eliminating legal practice or its human relationships.
pts.d: Jeff Steinberg describes AI-enabled access to information and its incorporation into workflows as an opportunity to rethink both the business and practice of law. He frames the change as continuing evolution at different speeds, rather than a categorical break. His expectation that legal practice persists rests on the continuing need to negotiate and adjudicate rules; he does not predict lawyer headcount reductions or wholesale autonomous substitution.

pts.k: Steinberg proposes combining machine-learning-derived insights with a generative-AI presentation layer to make historical firm data actionable and usable.
pts.d: He assigns the extraction of reliable factual insights to machine learning and deterministic business logic, and assigns context, explanation and visual presentation to generative AI. He claims this combination can avoid hallucinations, off-track outputs and bad citations while allowing attorneys to use trusted information without being slowed down. This is his proposed design approach and intended result, not a reported test demonstrating complete accuracy. He also identifies improved time capture with less effort as an intended benefit of tools built around historical time-entry information, although that particular statement does not specify an AI mechanism.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Steinberg supports his expectations principally with operating experience, historical analogies and preliminary customer conversations, not quantitative AI evaluations.
pts.d: He draws on building Redwood Analytics, the emergence of business-intelligence tools in the 2000s, digitising medical-record retrieval at Ontelis, and the earlier transition from paper to computerised accounting. His early conversations suggest heterogeneous AI adoption: some firms have embraced it but worry about technological instability, while others proceed cautiously. No AI benchmark, measured hallucination rate, controlled productivity study or quantified SurePoint customer outcome is offered for his claims. His observation that mid-market firms have remained resilient is a broader market assessment, not evidence isolating AI's effect. Sponsor advertisements and the host's references to company research are not treated as Steinberg's evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: AI-driven change is already underway in Steinberg's account, but he supplies no fixed transformation deadline and conditions adoption on reliability, usability, customer readiness and stable infrastructure.
pts.d: In this interview, labelled 2026, Steinberg is roughly ten days to two weeks into his role. He describes technology changing over the preceding twelve months and expects continuing evolution at different paces. His first-year priorities are understanding customers, balancing product stability with rapidly evolving insights, and building service and technology partnerships; these are priorities rather than dated AI deployment commitments. He seeks a 10–20-year useful life for core firm-performance software while allowing insight capabilities to change quickly. He treats deterministic factual foundations, appropriate business logic and practical delivery to users as conditions for the benefits he anticipates.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected group is mid-sized law firms, with distinct benefits envisaged for lawyers, financial leaders and administrative staff, and downstream efficiency benefits for clients.
pts.d: SurePoint's stated customer range is approximately 20–350 attorneys. Steinberg envisages attorneys and CFOs making better decisions from data, partners building practices and serving clients without unreliable outputs slowing them down, and timekeepers capturing work with less effort. He emphasises connecting front-office work with administrative workflows and tailoring functionality to different users and firm structures. His broader product objective is to help mid-market firms compete on efficiency and unit costs against larger firms while facing pressure from nimble smaller firms; he does not present an AI-specific measured cost advantage. Clients are described as downstream beneficiaries of efficiency, not as recipients of an access-to-justice intervention.
